dct_description_sm: Winter distribution, movements and areas of use are very poorly known for most marine birds.  This knowledge gap precludes efforts to understand the environmental influences that affect seabirds year-round, information that is critical to interpreting how they may adjust to changing ecosystem conditions and how they can be used as indicators of variation in the marine environment.  We used archival geolocators to track the location and behavior of common murres and thick-billed murres from 7 breeding colonies from the Canadian Arctic to Newfoundland and Labrador.  Preliminary results indicate that important marine wintering areas for these murres include the Labrador Sea, Davis Strait, the southwest coast of Greenland, the Grand Bank, and the Flemish Cap.  The importance of wintering areas differed between species and among colonies, with individuals showing similar, colony-specific patterns. The more northerly breeding Thick-billed Murres ranged  more widely in their oceanic habitat than Common Murres. This knowledge provides robust biological data both on important marine areas for seabirds and on seabird-habitat associations, which are critical for predicting likely influences of future climate change on populations of these top marine predators.
dct_title_s: Tracking Studies Reveal Winter Habitat  of Murres from Arctic Colonies in Eastern Canada
